The run loop is your Looper

On Android, the main thread runs a Looper: take a message from the queue, run it, repeat. iOS has the same idea under another name. Here it is, and the one way it differs.

    An iOS app moves through app states: not running, inactive, active, background, suspended. Seconds after it goes to the background it's suspended: still in memory, running no code. iOS can end a suspended app without running any of your code, so save your state as you enter the background, not at the end.

The problem

On Android, you know the main thread's routine: a Looper takes the next message from its queue, runs it to the end, and repeats, and nothing touches the screen from anywhere else. Your iOS screen also needs touches handled, timers fired and redraws done, one after another, on one thread. Who runs that loop on iOS?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

iOS calls it a run loop: an event processing loop. Every thread can have one, created the first time it's needed. It waits for work, a touch, a timer, a task from elsewhere; handles it; and when nothing is left, puts the thread to sleep until the next thing arrives. Same job as Android's Looper, same reason: one thread handles events one at a time, so nothing has to lock the screen.

You don't start the main one yourself: UIKit sets up and runs the run loop on the main thread when the app launches, the way Android's ActivityThread.main() starts the main Looper. Other threads only run their run loop if you start it.

And the rule you already know carries over exactly: screen work happens on the main thread, and anything slow you do there blocks the loop. A touch waits behind it, and the screen stops responding, iOS's version of jank.

The analogy

The same clerk from the Android house, with a different name on the badge: work from the in-tray, one item at a time, and doze off at the desk when the tray is empty.

Check yourself

On iOS, you read a large file on the main thread, and it takes 2 seconds. The user taps meanwhile. What happens?

Not quite. Touches are the main run loop's job; they wait behind your file read.

Right. One loop, one thing at a time.

Not quite. A run loop runs each piece of work to the end; it can't pause your read halfway.

Why does the main thread sleep when there's no work, instead of checking again and again?

Not quite. Nothing is ended: sleeping is what saves the CPU and battery.

Right. Sleep until there's work: no wasted CPU.

What's the difference between a run loop and a thread?

Right. Worker vs its routine.

Not quite. Any thread can have one; the main thread is only one of them.

Not quite. A run loop isn't a thread: any thread can have one, feeding it its events.

Sources
  • Apple: Threading Programming Guide, Run Loops ("A run loop is an event processing loop that you use to schedule work and coordinate the receipt of incoming events. The purpose of a run loop is to keep your thread busy when there is work to do and put your thread to sleep when there is none"; "each thread, including the application's main thread, has an associated run loop object… The app frameworks automatically set up and run the run loop on the main thread")

What you now know

Any iOS thread can have a run loop, and the main thread always does: an event loop that handles work when there is some and puts the thread to sleep when there is none. The app framework starts the main thread's run loop for you, just as Android starts the main Looper. UI work belongs on that loop, so blocking it freezes the screen.
